C. W. C. Oman argues that the Byzantine Empire was neither decadent nor monotonous [PDF p. 13]. He contends the empire played a vital role in resisting Saracens and preserving learning [PDF p. 13]. The history begins with Greek colonists from Megara founding Byzantium approximately 2,558 years ago [PDF p. 27]. These settlers established their colony on a headland near the Golden Horn [PDF p. 27]. Legend suggests the Delphic oracle instructed them to build opposite Chalcedon [PDF p. 29]. The city's location provided significant military and commercial advantages for controlling Black Sea trade [PDF p. 30-31]. After falling to Alexander the Great, Byzantium eventually became a free confederate city under Rome [PDF p. 34]. However, Emperor Vespasian later stripped the city of these privileges [PDF p. 34].

Emperor Constantine the Great besieged and captured the city in A.D. 323 [PDF p. 37-38]. Oman interprets Constantine as a practical leader seeking a convenient administrative center [PDF p. 39-41]. He chose Byzantium due to its superior military and commercial positioning [PDF p. 42-43]. Constantine established the new capital around A.D. 328 or 329 [PDF p. 54]. He held a consecration festival on May 11, 330, featuring Christian services [PDF p. 54]. The topography of Constantinople included a central marketplace and an imperial palace [PDF p. 44-45]. Public life centered on the Augustaeum and the Hippodrome [PDF p. 45-49]. Chariot racing in the Hippodrome fueled intense factional rivalries between the Blues and Greens [PDF p. 49]. These factions often caused public disorder and political instability [PDF p. 49-50].

The empire faced threats from Sapor of Persia and various northern groups [PDF p. 58]. By A.D. 376, Huns had driven the Visigoths toward the Roman Danube border [PDF p. 61]. Emperor Valens allowed the Goths to enter as subject-allies [PDF p. 62]. Corruption by officials like Lupicinus led to starvation and revolt [PDF p. 63]. This resulted in the Battle of Adrianople in A.D. 378, where Valens died [PDF p. 65, 67]. Theodosius later stabilized the region by enlisting Gothic war-bands into the Roman army [PDF p. 68]. Oman argues that using barbarian auxiliaries under their own chiefs was dangerous [PDF p. 70]. Following the death of Theodosius in A.D. 395, factional wars erupted between German and Roman parties [PDF p. 73].

Justinian ascended the throne in A.D. 527 after the death of his uncle [PDF p. 91]. His marriage to the former actress Theodora caused significant social scandal [PDF p. 92, 93]. Oman describes Justinian as a hard, suspicious, and tireless ruler [PDF p. 95]. In A.D. 532, the Nika riots erupted due to the Blue and Green factions [PDF p. 101]. Rebels attempted to install Hypatius as Caesar during this violent unrest [PDF p. 102]. Empress Theodora refused to flee, prompting a final assault by Belisarius [PDF p. 105]. This assault killed approximately 35,000 people in the Hippodrome [PDF p. 105-106]. Justinian then pursued foreign conquests, including the Vandal kingdom in Africa [PDF p. 107, 111]. Belisarius also invaded Italy to challenge the Ostrogoths [PDF p. 114]. Oman interprets the Gothic failure as a result of religious and racial tensions [PDF p. 109].

The later reign of Justinian was marred by a devastating plague starting in A.D. 542 [PDF p. 127]. Simultaneously, Chosroes of Persia launched an invasion that sacked Antioch [PDF p. 125]. Following Justinian's death, the empire faced threats from Lombards, Avars, and Slavs [PDF p. 141]. The Slavs used unconventional tactics like hiding in water to ambush Romans [PDF p. 149]. This instability contributed to the fall of Emperor Maurice in 602 [PDF p. 152-153]. Phocas captured and executed Maurice after a military revolt [PDF p. 153]. Oman characterizes Phocas as a brutal usurper whose reign caused imperial decay [PDF p. 154]. Heraclius took the throne in 610 to find an empire in chaos [PDF p. 156-157]. He eventually defeated the Persians and restored Roman territory by 628 [PDF p. 161, 164].

The recovery was short-lived as the Saracen invasion began [PDF p. 166]. The Arabs captured Syria and Egypt, including Jerusalem in 637 [PDF p. 189]. Constantine IV later defended Constantinople against an Arab siege using Greek-fire [PDF p. 196]. In 695, Leontius deposed Justinian II, who had been a reckless tyrant [PDF p. 199, 201]. This usurpation initiated twenty years of anarchy and constant revolts [PDF p. 202]. Justinian II eventually returned to power in 705 through Bulgarian support [PDF p. 205]. His restoration triggered a reign of terror that ended in 711 [PDF p. 205, 206]. Leo the Isaurian rose to power in 717 and defended Constantinople from Saracens [PDF p. 208, 211]. Leo also initiated the Iconoclastic movement to combat image-worship [PDF p. 215].

The Macedonian dynasty began with Basil the Macedonian [PDF p. 240]. This era saw a literary revival under rulers like Leo VI and Constantine VII [PDF p. 241]. The empire maintained strength through a commercial monopoly on the Bosphorus [PDF p. 251]. Nicephorus Phocas exploited Caliphate fragmentation to conquer Crete in 961 [PDF p. 253, 254]. John Zimisces later defeated a Russian invasion in 971 [PDF p. 260, 261]. Basil II conducted a long war against King Samuel and conquered Bulgaria [PDF p. 266, 268]. The Macedonian dynasty ended in 1057, triggering civil war and Turkish invasions [PDF p. 274, 275]. After the defeat at Manzikert in 1071, Alexius Comnenus stabilized the empire [PDF p. 277, 283]. However, the Crusades caused a terminal decline in Constantinople's commercial wealth [PDF p. 293, 294].

The empire passed to the incompetent Isaac and Alexius Angelus [PDF p. 300]. These rulers relied on rapacious favorites and auctioned public offices [PDF p. 302]. In 1203, the Fourth Crusade arrived due to Venetian interests [PDF p. 305]. The Crusaders established a Latin Empire that remained perpetually unstable [PDF p. 318]. Theodore Lascaris founded the Empire of Nicaea in 1206 [PDF p. 324]. Michael Paleologus finally reconquered Constantinople in 1261 [PDF p. 330]. The restored empire faced permanent territorial decay and Ottoman expansion [PDF p. 334, 341]. John Cantacuzenus further destroyed the empire by summoning Turkish aid [PDF p. 351-353]. The narrative concludes with the fall of Constantinople on May 29, 1453 [PDF p. 37
